maths_errors.text: A rhombus has 4 equal sides but angles are not 90°.
maths_errors.correction: A rhombus is any quadrilateral with 4 equal sides. Its angles need not be 90°, but they can be: a square is a special rhombus. Say instead: 'A rhombus has 4 equal sides; its angles do not have to be 90°. A square is a rhombus with right angles.'

maths_errors.text: That's the check — if n = 3 gives 180°, your formula is right.
maths_errors.correction: Checking one value does not prove a formula is right. For example, n × 60° also gives 180° when n = 3, and it is wrong for n = 4 (240° instead of 360°). Say: 'Check with a triangle (180°) and a quadrilateral (360°).'

missing_spec_content.spec_text: apply the properties of angles at a point, angles at a point on a straight line, vertically opposite angles
missing_spec_content.why: Only 'they form a straight line' appears in passing. The lesson does not teach angles at a point (360°), angles on a straight line (180°) or vertically opposite angles.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: understand and use alternate and corresponding angles on parallel lines
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not mention parallel-line angles at all.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: derive and use the sum of angles in a triangle (eg to deduce and use the angle sum in any polygon, and to derive properties of regular polygons)
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson assumes 180° for each triangle and never derives it. It also does not show how the triangle split gives (n − 2) triangles, or how to work out the properties of a regular polygon, such as finding n from an exterior angle.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: derive and apply the properties and definitions of: special types of quadrilaterals, including square, rectangle, parallelogram, trapezium, kite and rhombus
missing_spec_content.why: Parallelogram, trapezium and kite are never described. Square, rectangle and rhombus get only partial properties: no parallel sides, no symmetry, and no square or parallelogram diagonals.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: knowing names and properties of isosceles, equilateral, scalene, right-angled, acute-angled, obtuse-angled triangles
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not cover the types of triangle.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: knowing names and using the polygons: pentagon, hexagon, octagon and decagon
missing_spec_content.why: Decagon is not mentioned. Polygon names are not linked to their numbers of sides, except for the octagon in the worked example.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: identify properties of the faces, surfaces, edges and vertices of: cubes, cuboids, prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones and spheres
missing_spec_content.why: The concept slide says faces, edges and vertices matter but never teaches them. No 3D shape properties are given, including curved surfaces for the cylinder, cone and sphere.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: use conventional terms and notations: points, lines, vertices, edges, planes, parallel lines, perpendicular lines, right angles, polygons, regular polygons and polygons with reflection and/or rotation symmetries
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not define these terms or their notation, such as the arrow marks for parallel lines or the square symbol for a right angle. It does not cover reflection or rotation symmetry of polygons.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: use the standard conventions for labelling and referring to the sides and angles of triangles
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not teach labelling such as angle ABC or side AB.
The lesson does not cover this.

cases_not_modelled.case: Finding the number of sides of a regular polygon from a given exterior or interior angle
cases_not_modelled.why: This is a common question for 'derive properties of regular polygons'. The only worked example goes from n to the angles.

cases_not_modelled.case: Missing angle in an irregular polygon
cases_not_modelled.why: The commonMistakes slide says 'you need the individual angle values to find a missing one' but no example shows how.

density.text: Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°  |  Each interior angle of a regular polygon = (n − 2) × 180° ÷ n  |  Each exterior angle of a regular polygon = 360° ÷ n
density.why: Three formulas are packed onto one line, separated by bars. A first-time learner cannot easily tell which applies when.

density.text: Any polygon can be split into (n − 2) triangles, each contributing 180°, giving the total interior angle sum.
density.why: The reason for (n − 2) is not given. The student needs to be told the triangles are drawn from one vertex, which cannot join to itself or its two neighbours. There is also no diagram.

density.text: Learning the key properties of quadrilaterals (which sides are equal, which angles are equal, which diagonals bisect) saves time because you can read off information directly rather than calculating it.
density.why: One sentence carries several ideas. 'Which diagonals bisect' is unclear because it does not say what they bisect.

density.text: Using (n − 2) × 180 without subtracting 2 — writing n × 180 instead.
density.why: It states the correct formula and then says 'without subtracting 2', which is confusing on first read. Simpler: 'Writing n × 180° instead of (n − 2) × 180°.'

density.text: A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. A rhombus has 4 equal sides but angles are not 90°. A rectangle has equal diagonals; a rhombus has diagonals that bisect at right angles.
density.why: Three shapes and mixed side, angle and diagonal properties are in one fact. They are not organised shape by shape, so the student cannot see which properties each shape has.

density.text: Check using the exterior angle: 360° ÷ 8 = 45°. Interior + exterior should = 180°.
density.why: The calculation of the exterior angle is hidden in the instruction instead of the working. The reason the two angles add to 180° (they lie on a straight line) is not restated here.
